item.title: Saudi Arabia executes man over crimes allegedly committed as a child
item.description:
Saudi Arabia executes man over crimes allegedly committed as a child

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 10/20/2026 - 10:13
Human Rights Watch says Hassan al-Faraj was convicted over offences allegedly committed at 14, while Yousef al-Manasif faces execution after a Supreme Court ruling
Saudi Shia women during a protest against the execution of cleric Nimr al-Nimr in Qatif, Saudi Arabia, 8 January 2016 (STR/AFP)
Off

Saudi Arabia has executed a man convicted of offences allegedly committed when he was a child, according to Human Rights Watch (HRW).

Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, who was executed on Saturday, was convicted of offences allegedly committed when he was 14 years old, including "meeting and developing friendships with other detained and wanted individuals". 

“The execution of Hassan al-Faraj is unconscionable compounded by alleged torture-tainted evidence and a well-documented record of unfair trials,” said Joey Shea, HRW’s senior Saudi Arabia researcher.

“With the Supreme Court’s recent decision, Yousef al-Manasif is also at serious risk of execution,” she added.

Faraj was arrested in 2017 and sentenced to death by Saudi Arabia’s Specialised Criminal Court in 2022, according to HRW. 

His lawyers have said that he had been tortured and forced to sign a confession used in the case. HRW also reported that he was held in solitary confinement. 

Yousef al-Manasif, who was convicted over alleged offences committed when he was 15 and 16, is also at risk of execution after the Supreme Court reportedly upheld his sentence, according to the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights (ESOHR). 

Manasif was arrested in April 2017. He was accused of participating in protests against the Saudi authorities’ treatment of the country’s Shia minority and attending funeral processions in 2011 and 2012, when he was 15 and 16.

A 2024 opinion adopted by the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention found that the detention of Faraj, Manasif and three other men -  Jawad Qureiris, Abdullah al-Derazi and Jalal al-Labbad - was arbitrary and that their proceedings involved serious fair-trial violations.

It said their detention violated several provisions of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and called for their immediate release and compensation. 

Saudi Arabia’s government disputed the allegations, saying the claims were unfounded and that the country’s laws and procedures complied with international human rights standards.

The UN working group’s report said Manasif alleged that he had been physically and psychologically tortured in detention and coerced into signing confessions later used against him. 

Another defendant, Ali al-Mabyook, was sentenced to death over alleged offences that included attending funeral processions before he turned 18, according to HRW and court documents. 

Coerced confessions

His case has also drawn concern from rights groups over the use of counterterrorism legislation and allegations of coerced confessions. 

Qureiris was sentenced to death in 2022 over alleged offences that included acts committed as a minor, according to the UN working group.

The group’s opinion said he had alleged that he was tortured and held in solitary confinement for 270 days to force a confession.

Saudi authorities executed Ali al-Subaiti on 9 April 2026, according to the Saudi Press Agency.

HRW said he had been sentenced to death over alleged offences that included participating in a demonstration when he was 12. 

Saudi Arabia’s 2018 Juvenile Law and a 2020 executive order introduced protections against imposing the death penalty for certain offences committed by people under 18. 

HRW has argued that the protections do not adequately cover defendants prosecuted under the kingdom’s counterterrorism legislation, leaving some people convicted over alleged childhood offences at risk of execution. 

“Saudi Arabia’s execution spree, particularly for offences by children, shows no signs of slowing down in 2026,” Shea said.

“This underscores the urgent need for the international community to press the Saudi government to immediately halt executions and abolish the death penalty once and for all.”

item.title: Workers recruitment for Japan from 1 April 2027
item.description:
Japan will begin recruiting Bangladeshi workers from 1 April 2027 under a Memorandum of Cooperation on Employment Skills Development (ESDP-MOC) signed between the countries on 17 October.

The Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Ministry Secretary signed on behalf of Bangladesh while representatives of Japan’s Justice Ministry, Foreign Affairs Ministry, Health, Labour and Welfare Ministry and the National Police Agency signed on behalf of Japan, said a press release today, Monday.

The initial term of the agreement is five years, said the release, adding, it will automatically be extended for another five years upon expiry. As a result, the overall term of the agreement will be 10 years.

Under the agreement, protection of Bangladeshi workers will be ensured, cooperation between the two countries in sending and receiving workers will be strengthened and opportunities for skills development through employment will be created.

Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury said, through this agreement, in addition to ensuring maximum protection for Bangladeshi workers, opportunities will be created for their skills development, higher wages and long-term residence in Japan.

He said that under the agreement, Bangladeshi workers will receive legal protection equivalent to that of local Japanese workers and equal opportunities for men and women in the workplace will be ensured.

Particularly female foreign workers cannot be dismissed or subjected to discriminatory treatment because of pregnancy or childbirth. For this reason, the agreement also does not contain any mandatory provision for forced repatriation, the release said.

It further said that during Prime Minister Tareque Rahman’s upcoming visit to Japan, copies of the agreement will be officially handed over between the two parties.

The ministry expressed hope that through the implementation of the agreement, the friendly relations between Bangladesh and Japan will be further strengthened, and opportunities for the development of Bangladesh’s skilled human resources will be expanded.

item.title: Rooppur plant eyes power start-up in October
item.description:
The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant (RNPP) is set to begin the power start-up phase likely this October, a key step towards generating electricity from the country’s first nuclear power facility.
Once the reactor’s output reaches 35% of capacity, supply to the national grid will begin. Officials say that, if everything goes according to plan, around 300 megawatts (MW) could be added to the grid in December.
A responsible source at the Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Limited (NPCBL) told Dhaka Tribune that the start-up would begin at zero to 1% power likely on October 25. Once output reaches 35%, 300MW can be supplied to the grid, which is the standard procedure.
“But numerous tests must be carried out to clear each stage,” the source said. After every increase in power, all parameters must be checked to ensure they are within limits.
According to the sources, it usually takes about 40 days to reach 35% power after the start-up begins. The timeline could stretch if any test fails along the way.
If all goes well, the plant could be ready for production in the last week of November, or else in December, they said.
Currently, tests on B-2 (fission reaction) are underway. After these are completed, and subject to approval from the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA), Stage-C, which is the power start-up, will begin shortly.
Stage-D, or trial operation, will follow next. During this phase, the plant will be tested through trials to establish that it can operate at full capacity. Power generation will be raised and lowered to test the grid’s capacity to absorb it. The plant will also be shut down briefly at times for testing.
Stage-D is expected to take around 10 months. During this period, Rooppur’s operators will work alongside the Russian contractor to build up their skills.
The sources said the plant is currently in the physics start-up stage, with every piece of equipment being tested at very low thermal power. Thermal power will then be raised to spin the turbine, and electricity generation will begin gradually.
Power will be increased step by step once everything checks out in the physics tests and BAERA gives its approval. BAERA’s permission will also be required for spinning the turbine and for generating electricity. At that point, officials will check whether the turbine and the generation process are functioning properly.
An official responsible for the construction project told local media: “If we follow the ideal programme, we hope the plant can go into production by December. But if we get stuck on any test at the last moment, it could take longer.”
Some people involved in the project, however, expressed doubt about meeting the December schedule. They said it is very difficult to give a fixed date for a nuclear plant to start production, and that even a minor problem could mean restarting work from scratch. Even so, December will remain the target.
A delegation from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is organising a training workshop to help ensure emergency preparedness and safety at Rooppur, sources said.
The IAEA’s Emergency Preparedness Review (EPREV) mission will run in Bangladesh from November 8 to 18, reviewing the country’s preparedness for nuclear emergencies.
Talking to Dhaka Tribune, Md Anwar Hossain, secretary of the Ministry of Science and Technology, said bringing Rooppur’s emergency preparedness up to international standards would require coordination among the agencies concerned, trained manpower, clear written guidelines, and round-the-clock radiation and environmental monitoring.
BAERA Chairman Mahmudul Hasan said an integrated emergency response framework should be put in place before the IAEA delegation’s visit, with clearly defined responsibilities for everyone, from first responders in the field to national-level decision-makers.
Abul Khayer Md Akkas Ali, additional secretary of the Atomic Energy Division at the Science and Technology Ministry, said the government is committed to providing the necessary institutional support to ensure nuclear safety.
Meanwhile, earlier, Posts, Telecommunications, ICT Minister and Science and Technology Minister Fakir Mahbub Anam said efforts are under way to supply around 300MW from Rooppur’s first reactor to the national grid by November.
He said the 1,200MW mega project is a flagship project for Russia’s Rosatom, which is therefore giving it high priority. Experts sent three months ago are working round the clock, he added.
The minister also said there is a plan to load fuel into the second reactor around June next year.

item.title: Nationwide meat recall underway as ‘temperature abuse’ impacts 1.5 million pounds of beef, pork, and chicken
item.description:
A massive recall involving more than 1.5 million pounds of meat product was announced this weekend after the manufacturer discovered what the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) deemed to be possible “temperature abuse.”

Here’s what that means, what meat products are affected, and what you should do if you have any of the recalled items.

What’s happened?

On Saturday, the USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service alerted the public about a voluntary recall by Kayem Foods Inc., a more-than-a-century-old meat products company based in Chelsea, Massachusetts.

The recall involves more than 1.5 million pounds of meat products produced by Kayem Foods. According to the FSIS, Kayem is recalling 1,584,361 pounds of ready-to-eat (RTE) meat and poultry products over fears that impacted products “may have experienced temperature abuse during storage.”

The problem was discovered after one of Kayem Foods’ retail customers complained about warm product temperatures related to some of the meat products, the notice states.

Kayem then investigated the claims and found one of the warehouse coolers where the products were stored “experienced temperature deviations,” according to the FSIS.

What is “temperature abuse”?

While the term “temperature abuse” makes it sound like someone knowingly altered the meats’ temperature, the situation is actually less nefarious.

In relation to this recall, “temperature abuse” simply means that the products’ temperatures deviated from what they should have been stored at, potentially making the products unsafe to eat.

In a recall notice posted directly on Kayem Foods’ website, the company says that the issue was due to “a cooling system malfunction at one of the company’s warehouses that resulted in storage temperature deviations.” 

Announcing the recall, Kayem CEO Matt Monkiewicz said, “Our business depends on providing consumers with safe food of the highest quality. Out of an abundance of caution, we are undertaking this voluntary recall.”

He added: “We take food safety very seriously and apologize to our valued consumers. Our management team takes full responsibility. We have learned from and corrected the issue and will not allow this to happen again.” 

What products are included in the recall?

The more than 1.5 million pounds of meat products impacted by the recall include items sold under nine different brands:

  • Al Fresco
  • Deutschmacher
  • Essem
  • Genoa
  • Jordan’s
  • Kayem
  • McKenzie
  • Triple M
  • Winnisimmet

The products include numerous ready-to-eat items, such as sausages, chicken, pork, bacon, and other products. 

The FSIS says the recalled products bear the establishment numbers “EST. M/P 7839,” “EST. P 20935A” and “EST. M 9520” inside the USDA mark of inspection.

Items included in the recall “were produced approximately March 31, 2026, to Oct. 7, 2026.” Kayem Foods says the items were “stored and shipped between June 7, 2026, and October 14, 2026.”

The FSIS has published a full list of the items on its website. The agency has also published photos of the product packaging.

Kayem Foods has published its own list of recalled items here.

Where were the recalled products sold?

Neither the FSIS nor Kayem Foods has announced which retailers sold the recalled products. However, the FSIS says that the “items were shipped to retail and foodservice locations Nationwide and Hong Kong.”

The agency says that, as of the time of its notification, there have been no confirmed reports of anyone becoming ill from eating the recalled items.

What should I do if I have the recalled products?

The FSIS says consumers should check their refrigerators, as the items could still reside there even if purchased long ago. 

Consumers who have the recalled items are being urged not to consume them, but instead dispose of them or return them to their place of purchase.

Those with questions about the recall can contact Kayem Foods Customer Service at 800-426-6100 or email the company at info@kayem.com.

item.title: ‘The last bastion is gone’: the US right idolised Orbán’s Hungary. Can they recover now he has fallen?
item.description:
Over the past decade, Hungary has been a beacon for the ‘postliberal’ right, with pro-Trump thinkers making regular pilgrimages to Budapest. Now Orbán is gone, how will the movement adapt?

  • A longer version of this article first appeared in The Drift

Espresso Embassy, a third-wave coffee shop in Budapest’s diplomatic and governmental quarter, is where visiting reporters and academics come to talk politics. On the way in for my morning coffee on 18 March, I passed a poster for Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party that had been vandalised with a marker pen: “the safe choice” had become “the certain way to get fucked”. From across the cafe, I spotted the American journalist and historian Anne Applebaum locked in conversation, possibly with a source. I heard someone exclaim: “Just like Mussolini!” It was election season in Hungary.

It was also a couple of days before Cpac Hungary, a satellite event of the US-based conservative conference. As members of the international right arrived in town, the notorious Orbánist thinktank known as the Danube Institute was hosting an event called On Censorship, Tolerance, the Left and God. The official line would be: bad, good, bad, good.

item.title: The U.S. Army’s Pacific Strategy Depends on Allies
item.description:
“We never fight alone. We've never done that. You can go all the way back to the days of Revolutionary War. The United States has never gone into conflict on its own. We've always built coalitions. We've always involved partners and allies. And we'll continue to do so going forward.”

That was Gen. Ronald P. Clark, Commanding General, U.S. Army Pacific Command, speaking last Tuesday at a contemporary military forum, Decisive Landpower -- Deterrence and Partner Integration Against the Pacing Threat, as part of the 2026 Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Conference in Washington, D.C.

On the panel with Clark was Army Gen. Xavier T. Brunson, Commander, United Nations Command, U.S. Forces Korea, and Tara Murphy Dougherty, Chief Executive Officer of Air, a leading AI software firm that specializes in national security readiness.

The two Army generals spent a good deal of their time talking about lessons learned from Ukraine and the benefits to the U.S. of allies – specifically in the Pacific. That struck me as something to further explore, since one day later, on Wednesday, President Trump continued his running criticism of allies with an October 14, Truth Social screed.

Trump said in part: “Because of the fact that we have had such Military Success, we no longer ‘need,’ or desire, the NATO Countries’ assistance — WE NEVER DID! Likewise, Japan, Australia, or South Korea. In fact, speaking as President of the United States of America, by far the Most Powerful Country Anywhere in the World, WE DO NOT NEED THE HELP OF ANYONE! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP.”

On the other hand, Gen. Brunson had told the AUSA audience one day earlier, “Everything that we do is intricately woven around the ROK (Republic of Korea)-U.S. alliance. That alliance has stood for some 75 years and it is an example or a paragon, if you will, of all that's right when folk work in alliance together. The problems that we solve are joint problems. They're not just U.S. problems. They're not just Republic of Korea problems. What they are is great opportunities for two nations to work in concert with one another in order to arrive at solutions that are beneficial for both countries.”

Gen. Clark explained further, “So our ability to be able to work with partners and allies on their sovereign soil, to be able to share procedures that we build through [military] exercises over the course of a year, some joint, some army-to-army, but always integrated with our partners. It gives us the opportunity to have our systems work technically, to have our procedures nested, and to get to know one another in a way that allows us to build the trust that's necessary in training. Because if we wait until crisis or conflict, it's too late to ask the question, can I trust

you? But because we've been working together, because we've exercised at scale, because we're modernizing our forces alongside one another, it works.”

Clark added, “We've really worked hard at building those relationships at scale inside of the land forces. We have a land forces dialogue that meets multiple times a year -- chiefs of army of Australia, Japan, the Philippines, and the U.S. We've invited the ROKs in, we've invited India in, and it continues to grow. So those relationships built army-to-army are what allows us to really integrate across interoperability, and integrate it really across our formations and with our partners in all.”

Brunson described how he and Korean Gen. Kim Sung-min, Deputy Commander of the U.S.-ROK Combined Forces Command, discussed training differently “taking advantage of the knowledge that we have of the threats that exist or that prevail in the Ukraine fight.”

Brunson said, “We talk about how we would operate in a distributed fashion…Just imagine if we trained across the entirety of the [Korean] Peninsula and got ourselves in a shape where we would say you can't utilize the things that you've learned in the fight in the battlefield in Ukraine on us, because we learned the same lessons and we've distributed ourselves in such a way that we don't make ourselves the target. We won't be moored in place.”

Clark talked about Russia, North Korea and China “learning from watching us partner, but the partnerships that our adversaries have built are transactional versus the transformational relationships that we build as a security partner of choice globally…for us it's really transformational relationships that we look to cultivate with partners and allies over time.”

Brunson described how the North Koreans, fighting for the Russians in Ukraine were “able to test systems there…and then bring that back home. So, in one aspect, they've shortened their RDT&E cycle.” He also pointed out, “The fact that you have a combat trained force with recent

combat on the [Korean] Peninsula for the first time since 1953..[and] are now bringing those lessons learned back into their own training cycle, it's shortened their time to develop them.”

Clark said that U.S. forces had also learned from Ukraine about the need for mobility and camouflage, which he described as “age-old army forgotten sciences of how to hide in plain sight and how to camouflage ourselves from observation...Our ability to be able to use electronic warfare, to be able to use just good, old-fashioned camouflage and the ability to deceive our adversary is a must. In those two theaters [Ukraine and Iran] it's not a near-peer adversary that we would be working against -- whereas, in our theater [the Pacific] it absolutely is.”

For Clark, the questions were: “How do we fight, you know, Type One, Type Two UAS [unmanned aerial system, drones]; how do we think through ballistic missile defense holistically in the region. We spend a lot of time working again with the joint force for solutions associated with that. How do we maneuver?”

Brunson raised a new issue by pointing out that, “Our old system was something [a weapons system] breaks, we send it all the way back CONUS [Continental U.S.] in order to fix it so we can then bring it all the way back out again.” That used to take 29 days by ship.

However, he added, “In the ally that we have in Korea we have a an absolutely premier industrial base, if you look at the Korea defense industry, some of the kit that we're producing right now sits along our friends, allies and partners.” Brunson said, “The Army’s new infantry squad vehicle (ISV), for example, is produced by GM Defense and GM Defense is also in the Republic of Korea.”

“So the idea of a regional sustainment hub would simply be…to bring those means of production to the theater,” Brunson suggested, noting, “In the maritime domain, when we look at maintenance, repair, and overhaul, which is being done forward alongside the Koreans, you know that 15 percent of global ship building is done in Korea. And, oh by the way, we've got an ally with a mutual defense treaty in Japan that has 10% of global ship building. And if we take these cases forward, we're able to stay in theater longer.”

The answer, Brunson said, “We've got to try to achieve admirable endurance in theater by partnering alongside our allies, seeing the things that they can do better than we can right now at distance and then keeping them right where they belong. That keeps our [military] forces forward.”

Dougherty chipped in saying: “Tens of millions of dollars saved by simply identifying things like unfilled requisitions or parts that are obsolete that can be replaced with something not obsolete and also less expensive. I think that this is it. This is part of how you generate lethality. You get readiness to pay for itself, because otherwise sustainment is too expensive when it has to be done for the entirety of the joint force all the way on the other side of the world.”

At one point, Clark said, “The secret sauce for us as an Army is our Non-Commissioned Officer (NCO) corps, reflecting Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s September 30 speech praising the same group.

Clark noted that both he and Brunson were sons of NCOs, and that “with the assistance of our senior non-commissioned officers, senior enlisted leaders across the [PACOM] region have embarked upon conducting assessments with our partners and developing strategies to help them build their NCO development programs inside of their formations.”

To illustrate his point, Clark said his units had just finished an assessment in Cambodia of its army and the Commander, Gen. Mao Sophan, “basically said, ‘Hey, whatever you're asking us to do, we're going to do it because we want to get to a level of proficiency with our Non-Commissioned Officer core that we see in yours.’"

I must point out that during the one-hour-and-thirty-minute session neither General -- Clark nor Brunson -- came near to mentioning President Trump’s repeated critical views about U.S. allies.

The closest anyone came was Dougherty, who at one point said diplomatically, “We'll head into midterm elections here [in the U.S.] in November, obviously as you know, and I think we expect some variation in the political dynamic in the United States, and our allies and partners all navigate their own political changes as well.”

She then added, “If you look over the course of history, however, at least modern history, certainly the United States has invested in those partnerships. And today, we still are -- maybe with a different flavor or a different attitude. And that's not really for me to say. I'm simply observing. But we haven't lost sight of the importance of allies and partners to securing U.S. national interests.”

I would bet Clark and Brunson – along with most U.S. military professionals – would silently agree with her statement.

item.title: The Hidden Risks of AI-Powered Intelligence
item.description:
Picture an intelligent analyst's screen. Data about troop movements, a port closure, a terrorist attack, or a weapons transfer sits at the center of a clean interface, with a confidence indicator glowing green. Two hundred outlets are carrying it, and the platform has counted every one. It looks like a corroboration. In many cases, it is a single Telegram post, copied, translated, summarized, and republished until its origin disappeared behind its own echo.

Nobody must be negligent for this to happen. It is what you get when a product or platform is built to measure volume and the user is tempted to read volume as truth.

I say this as someone who works with open-source material and believes in it. Commercial imagery, ship-tracking data, procurement records, leaked databases, and social media have changed what is knowable about conflicts and illicit networks; but the market that has grown up around these sources is selling something different from the discipline that makes them valuable, and governments and companies are buying it without noticing the difference.

A Crowded Market and a Thin Product

Open-source intelligence platforms are multiplying quickly. Walk through the company stands at any security conference and you will find dozens of them, each promising to fuse, monitor, and surface threats across the open internet, now almost always with an AI layer that summarizes, ranks, and alerts.

Strip away the interface and most of them offer little that a competent analyst couldn't already do with a search engine, a handful of specialist tools, and some patience. Reverse image searching, scraping social platforms, pulling corporate registry data, and geolocating an image are all learnable skills, and many of the best practitioners picked them up in public, often as volunteers. What the platforms add is convenience and scale, which is genuinely useful, but convenience is not analysis. The real product, in most cases, is the dashboard.

Dashboards are persuasive by design. They squeeze a messy information environment into something that looks like a picture of the world, with counts, trend lines, heat maps, and sentiment scores. Each of those findings implies that someone has already done the hard work of deciding what matters and what is true. Usually, no one has. The system has counted things, and counting is the easy part.

Counting Sources Is Not Testing Them

The core flaw is in what these systems reward. They tend to measure the number of sources behind a claim, not the independence of those sources. The two are very different things.

Independence is the foundation of corroboration. Two witnesses who saw an event separately make a claim stronger. Two witnesses who heard about it from the same third person do not. The same logic applies to reporting. A claim that traces back to a single channel but appears in two hundred outlets has one source and two hundred echoes.

Intelligence tradecraft has a name for this: circular reporting. It is among the oldest and best-documented ways analysts go wrong. The failures that most damaged the credibility of Western intelligence in the past generation involved, among other things, uncorroborated claims that were repeated, cross-referenced, and eventually treated as established because they seemed to come from many places. The lesson drawn at the time was that provenance matters more than prevalence. An aggregator that treats prevalence as confirmation is rebuilding the vulnerability that analysts spent years learning to guard against.

AI makes this problem fourfold. First, language models summarize and synthesize, and in doing so they take away the provenance trail that an analyst needs. A fluent paragraph that blends fifteen sources does not tell you that twelve of them are derivative. Second, the cost of generating plausible content has collapsed. Fabricated articles, cloned news sites, and coordinated amplification networks can now create the appearance of breadth cheaply, which is exactly the signal these platforms are built to count. Third, as more web content is produced or recycled by automated systems, the pool that analytics tools draw from becomes more self-referential. The echo chamber is increasingly populated by machines quoting each other. Lastly, AI can make uncertainty harder to see. Language models are designed to produce coherent answers, not to preserve the ambiguity of the evidence on which those answers are based. Contradictory sources can be reconciled into a smooth narrative, gaps can disappear beneath plausible inference, and tentative conclusions can acquire the tone of established fact. The danger is therefore not simply that an analyst receives false information, but that the uncertainty surrounding otherwise legitimate information becomes less visible.

None of this means the technology is useless. Entity extraction, translation, deduplication, and pattern detection across large data sets are real contributions. But the same tools that can help trace a claim to its origin are too often deployed to certify it instead.

Information Is Not Intelligence

The deeper problem is what happens after the dashboard produces its output. Companies market it as intelligence, and buyers, including government agencies, intelligence firms, financial institutions, and corporate security teams, purchase it as intelligence, then act on it.

However, open-source material is raw information. It becomes intelligence only after a process that no interface can fully automate. Someone has to establish where the material came from, grade how reliable the source has been, assess how credible the specific claim is, and test it against other collection. Established standards exist for this. Grading systems that rate source reliability separately from information credibility have been used for decades, and analytic standards require analysts to describe the quality and credibility of their sources, to distinguish between underlying evidence and judgment, and to account for alternative explanations. These are not bureaucratic formalities. They are the mechanism by which an organization knows how much weight a conclusion can bear.

When that step is skipped, the result is aggregated internet content with a confident interface. The output reads like a finished product, but the epistemic work behind it is missing, and the person reading it often can't see that. A decisionmaker shown a green indicator does not know whether it reflects three independent confirmations or one rumor with good distribution.

The consequences are practical. A government that bases sanctions designations, force posture, or diplomatic messaging on an unverified claim risks embarrassment at best and escalation at worst. A company that reroutes shipments or exits a market because a risk platform flagged a rumor can lose real money; and an agency that comes to rely on commercial feeds may quietly stop investing in the capabilities that would let it check them.


What Should Change

I would offer the following two principles.

One, to treat provenance and independence as essential to intelligence. Open-source material should be treated as a cue and a corroborator, not a conclusion. Open sources are at their best when they point collection in a useful direction or when they test and strengthen what other sources have suggested. A satellite image that shows construction at a site tells analysts where to look and what to ask. A procurement database entry might confirm a pattern already suspected. Neither is a finding on its own. The workflow should run from open-source lead to targeted collection to assessment, not from dashboard alert to briefing slide. As AI makes it easier to summarize, reproduce and generate information, analysts need to know not only what a source says, but where the information originated and whether apparently separate sources are actually independent. A fluent paragraph that blends fifteen sources does not tell an analyst that twelve of them are derivative. Likewise, a cluster of articles, websites or database entries may create the appearance of broad corroboration while ultimately tracing back to a single underlying claim. Platforms should therefore preserve provenance wherever possible and make the distinction between original reporting, derivative content and AI-generated material visible to the user. The workflow should run from open-source lead to targeted collection to assessment, not from dashboard alert to briefing slide.

Two, protect human assessment and the collection that supports it. AI can make uncertainty harder to see. Language models are designed to produce coherent answers, not to preserve the ambiguity of the evidence on which those answers are based. Contradictory sources can be reconciled into a smooth narrative, gaps can disappear beneath plausible inference, and tentative conclusions can acquire the tone of established fact. Human analysts therefore need both the time and the authority to question what automated systems produce rather than simply validate it. That also means protecting the collection capabilities that AI cannot replace. As open-source material becomes more abundant, the value of what cannot be found online rises. Human sources, financial intelligence, law enforcement access and legal process take years to cultivate and moments to lose. A budget cycle that trims them in favor of subscriptions is trading durable capability for a license that expires. The objective should not be to remove automation from intelligence work, but to ensure that automation remains subordinate to collection, verification and human judgment.

What Open Sources Cannot Close

I learned the limits of open-source work firsthand while researching foreign components in Russian strike drones. Open sources got me a long way. Recovered wreckage data, teardown imagery, part markings, and manufacturer documentation could establish what was inside these systems and who made it. That is valuable, and it was achievable by skilled analysts working in public.

But the questions that mattered most were different. Who actually bought a given part? Through which intermediaries did it move? Who paid for it, and through which accounts? Those gaps could not be closed by any amount of scraping. They required the tools that sit behind a legal threshold or inside a trusted relationship: law enforcement access to shipping and customs records, financial intelligence on transactions, and human sources with knowledge of how the networks operate. A dashboard could tell us a component existed. Only that other collection could tell us how it got there and who was responsible, which is the information policymakers need if they want to disrupt the supply chain rather than simply describe it.

That experience shaped how I think about the current issue. Open sources and closed collection are not competitors. The first made the second more efficient, because it let investigators ask better questions. The second made the first more meaningful, because it turned an interesting observation into an attributable finding. Treating either as a substitute for the other would have left us with a weaker product.

Defending the Analytical Craft

None of this is an argument against open-source intelligence. It is an argument for it, properly understood.

The practitioners who built the field's reputation, whether in newsrooms, nonprofits, academia, or government, are rigorous precisely because they distrust easy answers. They document their methods, show their chains of evidence, and say so when something can't be confirmed. That culture is the real asset. It is also what the commercial market is most at risk of undermining, because rigor is slow and expensive to sell, while a dashboard can be demoed in ten minutes.

The test I would offer any buyer, policymaker, or analyst is simple. When you are shown a claim, ask where it began, who else has independent knowledge of it, and what other collection could confirm or contradict it. If the system in front of you cannot answer those questions, it hasn't given you intelligence. It has given you a well-organized rumor.

The volume of open information will keep growing, and the tools to process it will keep improving. The scarce resource will not be data. It will be judgment, along with the access and tradecraft that make judgment possible. Agencies and firms that remember that, and invest accordingly, will see more clearly than those who confuse a full screen with a full picture.

item.title: OpenAI expands ChatGPT ads to 26 more countries, including Pakistan, in bid to boost revenue
item.description:
OpenAI said on Wednesday it was expanding advertising on ChatGPT to 26 more countries, including Pakistan, ​bringing the total to 89 as ‌the AI company beefs up its advertising business to boost revenue ahead of a potential initial public ​offering.

The company said in August its ads ​business had reached an annualised revenue run ⁠rate of $1 billion.

OpenAI began testing ads in ChatGPT ​in the US earlier this year, and ​more than 100,000 advertisers have since run campaigns on the platform, the company said.

The expansion adds 14 more ​Latin American countries, including Argentina, Chile, Colombia ​and Peru, following launches in Mexico and Brazil.

Ads are also launching in markets across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia, including Nigeria, South Africa, Serbia, Ukraine, Cambodia, Bangladesh and Pakistan.

Advertisers can access ​ChatGPT ads ​in the ⁠new markets through technology partners, or get self-service access via Ads Manager ​on the company’s platform.

Ads will appear ​only ⁠on ChatGPT’s Free and Go plans, while Plus, Pro and Enterprise subscriptions will remain ad-free.

In ⁠September, ​OpenAI introduced AI-powered tools for ​advertisers and began testing business-sponsored agents with select US advertisers.

item.title: Fear as Indians struggle to prove voting rights
item.description:
Laddli Khatun pulled one document after another from a yellow bag, desperately hoping one would be enough to keep her name on India’s electoral rolls.

As the world’s largest democracy overhauls its voter lists, millions like Khatun are scrambling to re-establish their credentials, despite having voted before.

Critics and opposition parties say the exercise risks mass disenfranchisement, and those removed fear wider citizenship repercussions.

More than 133 million names — including 28 million listed as dead — have been cut from rolls, according to figures reported by Indian media and cited by opposition parties in court filings.

Protests have rocked New Delhi, with demonstrators demanding the chief election commissioner’s resignation, alleging the overhaul is designed to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The Election Commission of India (ECI), a constitutional body, denies wrongdoing and says the revision complies with the law.

‘Burden of proof’

The Special Intensive Revision (SIR) requires voters to link themselves —directly or through their parents or grandparents —to electoral rolls from 2002-03, the last time such a rigorous review took place.

Khatun, 39, was not of voting age at the time. So she must now prove that at least one of her parents or grandparents featured on those rolls.

“My parents died when I was a baby,” Khatun, who lives in a Delhi slum, told AFP at a hearing reviewing voter credentials.

“They were poor unlettered people who left no documents behind.” Many face Khatun’s predicament.

“Women, minorities, people living at the margins and the poorest are the worst hit by this exercise, because they find it very difficult to produce documents which can prove their citizenship,” said transparency activist Anjali Bhardwaj.

The Election Commission previously sought to enrol eligible voters through door-to-door visits, guided by its motto: “No voter to be left behind”.

Critics say the exercise shifts the “burden of proof” onto voters.

“The methodology followed has been of physical door-to-door verification,” former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told AFP.

“It was never that you asked people wholesale to establish their eligibility all over again… after they have been admitted to the rolls through the prescribed due process.”

‘Untraceable’

Surajmukhi, made homeless when an eviction drive demolished the slum where she had lived for 30 years, was removed from Delhi’s draft rolls and marked “untraceable”.

“I have no document to link myself to the 2002 voter rolls, because at the time I was not enrolled as a voter, and my parents are long dead,” she said, standing in the rubble of her home.

“But I have voted multiple times since — the officials themselves came to our home and enrolled us as voters. What has suddenly changed?” Officials on the ground acknowledge the difficulties the exercise poses for poorer voters.

“Mapping yourself to the 2002 voter lists is not easy for those who are not educated and technologically savvy,” said Mukesh Khanna, a booth-level officer in a Delhi suburb with a large population of working-class migrants.

Special camps have been set up to help voters, but many still struggle to navigate the process.

‘Suspicious’

Millions have also been flagged for additional checks after the Election Commission used automated systems to identify what it calls “logical discrepancies”, including mismatched names and inconsistent family details.

Independent analyses suggest Muslims have been disproportionately affected.

In Delhi, an analysis by The Hindu newspaper found Muslims accounted for around 20 per cent of voters flagged, compared with 13.6pc of the electorate.

The disparity was even starker in West Bengal, according to the Kolkata-based policy think tank Sabar Institute.

Street cleaner Shahida, 42, received a notice because her mother was only 15 years older than her — an age gap the software flagged as “suspicious”.

“What am I expected to do — go back in time and ask my dead grandparents why they got my dead mother married so young?” she said.

“The reality is child marriages were common among the poor at the time.” National rugby player and actor Aslam, 24, who uses one name, said his voter registration was flagged as “suspicious” because six other people were linked to his deceased father, according to a notice seen by AFP.

“It is clearly targeted against voters who don’t vote for the BJP,” said Aslam, a Muslim with six siblings.

“It almost feels like the idea is to create a category of second-class citizens.” Modi’s Hindu-nationalist BJP, which strongly backs the revision, has long alleged that undocumented migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh — particularly Muslims — have fraudulently entered electoral rolls.

The Supreme Court has said exclusion from electoral rolls does not establish that someone is a foreign national.

However, Indian media have reported cases in West Bengal in which people excluded from voter rolls were accused of being undocumented migrants from Bangladesh, detained and, in some instances, pushed across the border.

For Khatun, the prospect of such an outcome hangs over an already gruelling ordeal.

“I have provided document after document, everything that I have,” she said. But what if they still ask us to leave the country?

Dengue: 5 more die, 1,366 hospitalized in 24hrs
item.description:
Five people died of dengue, and 1,366 new patients were hospitalized across the country in the 24 hours leading up to Tuesday morning.
With the latest fatalities, the dengue death toll has risen to 357 in the country this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Of the new deaths, two were reported in the Dhaka North City Corporation area and Barisal division each and one was recorded in Rangpur division, it said.
Of the total fatalities, 53.1% were female and 46.9% were male.
Since January 1 this year, hospitals across the country have admitted 115,617 dengue patients. Of them, 109,316 have recovered.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,204 as three die in 24 hours
item.description:
Three more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Tuesday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,204.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all three of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,100, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 104, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
The three new suspected fatalities were reported across three divisions; Dhaka, Mymensingh, and Chittagong with one death each.
A total of 1,217 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Tuesday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 215,768.
During the same period, 42 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 23,199.
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 191,761 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 184,168 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS.

item.title: 30 Bangladeshis return home after release from Cambodia detention centre
item.description:
Thirty Bangladeshi nationals who were released from an immigration detention centre in Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia, returned home on Tuesday.
They arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at around 12:15pm on a Thai Airways flight.
The returnees are Mohammad Harun Or Rashid, Mohammad Abdul Wadud, Mohammad Tarlib Hasan Titul, Sumit Chandra Das, Rakib Hossain, Bappi Das, Mohammad Labon Sheikh, Mohammad Abdur Rahman, Mohammad Billal Hossain, Mohammad Mostafa, Nur Nabi, Mohammad Emon Ali, Mohammad Barkatullah, Mohammad Rubel Mia, Ali Ahmed, Zahidul Islam, Shamsul Alam, Mohammad Abdur Rahman, Abu Jaher Sabuj, Shawon, Nahid Dhali, Raju Hossain, Mohammad Tayeb Ali Sheikh, Saimon Bhuiyan, Mohammad Rashedul, Mohammad Akash Ahmed, Mohammad Shimul Ali, Ashikur Rahman, Mohammad Alamin PK and Mohammad Kabir.
The Bangladeshis had travelled to Cambodia in search of jobs but became stranded at various scam centres in the country.
They registered to return home after the Cambodian government offered them the opportunity to leave without paying fines.
Accordingly, they arrived at Phnom Penh Airport on September 3. However, during immigration checks, Cambodian immigration police detained 32 Bangladeshis over various complications, including irregular immigration status.
Two were subsequently released, while the remaining 30 were held at the immigration detention centre.
Following an application by an organization named Anirban Survivor Voice Foundation, the first secretary of the labour wing at the Bangladesh Embassy in Bangkok was asked to take the necessary steps to secure the detainees’ release and facilitate their early return home.
After the required procedures were completed in phases, the 30 Bangladeshis returned to Bangladesh on Tuesday.

item.title: India’s Russian oil in focus as Rubio visits major Reliance refinery
item.description:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio kicks off a three-day visit to India on Monday in the finance hub of Mumbai, before heading to Jamnagar, home to a major oil refinery owned by industrial titan Reliance Industries.
Rubio’s business-oriented visit comes as trade talks remain stalled amid continued ambiguity on punitive measures from the US over India’s purchases of Russian oil.
Reliance is a top buyer of Venezuelan oil. The refinery can process 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, so it’s a valuable exporter of diesel fuel for global markets. The refinery has also been a major buyer of Russian Urals crude, making it a significant part of India’s energy relationship with Russia.
In March, Washington unveiled plans for a new oil refinery in Texas, backed by Reliance.
US President Donald Trump has put the value of the project at $300 billion (€258 billion) and presented it as a way to help reduce the US trade deficit with India. Whether the project moves forward, and on what terms, will be closely watched.
Since taking office for a second time in 2025, Trump has gone back and forth on tariff threats with India over what he considers to be unfair trade practices, along with India’s continued purchases of Russian oil amid the war in Ukraine.
In February 2026, Trump announced a “trade deal” that slashed US tariffs on Indian goods, in exchange for India lowering trade barriers and halting purchases of Russian oil. Trump had claimed that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi promised to stop buying Russian oil. However, this has never been confirmed by New Delhi.
While maritime data from Kpler, a commodities and energy-market intelligence company, showed Indian refiners briefly diversified supply away from Russia to avoid tightening sanctions, India’s deep reliance on discounted Russian crude continues to be a cornerstone of its energy strategy. Russia remains India’s top supplier of crude oil.
In mid-September, Trump signed the “Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act,” imposing 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian oil and gas, which includes India.
However, last week, just days before the legislation was due to go into effect, Trump signed an executive order pausing the sanctions.
Before traveling to India, Rubio was in Uzbekistan for a meeting of the “C5+1” diplomatic platform comprising the US and five Central Asian countries. In remarks on the sidelines, Rubio said trade talks with India are taking place with the sanctions waivers in mind.
“We have had to waive sanctions over the past few months, looking at the global supplies, looking at global prices, and the impact it was having on other countries,” he said.
“We’re trying to finalize a trade deal with India right now. We’re very close to doing that,” Rubio added.
In an interview with Indian broadcaster NDTV, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said that Jamnagar could be a valuable source of diesel for the US.
Foreign policy analyst C Raja Mohan of Jindal Global University in India told DW that Rubio skipping a visit to the Indian capital in favor of Mumbai and Jamnagar should not be considered a diplomatic snub, as the refinery has international importance amid the global energy crunch brought on by the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
He said Jamnagar is an “important node in global trade” because it processes Russian oil and serves as a conduit for refined Russian petroleum products reaching Western markets.
Although Trump’s sanctions reprieve offers New Delhi temporary relief, the underlying threat remains. Washington retains the option of imposing punitive tariffs, leaving Russian oil as a potential source of leverage in wider trade negotiations.
Former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautioned against reading too much into Rubio’s decision to skip Delhi amid political criticism in India.
“The focus of his current trip is on energy, and he is visiting the Reliance refinery in Jamnagar,” she told DW. “The high price of fuel, particularly diesel, has become a political liability for the Trump administration, which wants to be seen taking action on this issue.”
Diesel prices have skyrocketed around the world following the Iran war and the ensuing disruption of supply from the Middle East. In waiving Russia sanctions, Trump has tried to blame Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities as being the cause of high prices.
Shankar pointed to Reliance’s proposed Texas refinery, noting that the state is “one of the states in play” in the upcoming midterm elections in the US.
“Some forward movement on the investment would be welcome,” she said.
The two governments continue to describe their ties as a comprehensive global strategic partnership spanning defense, trade, technology and energy.
Analyst Mohan argued that describing the US-India relationship as uniquely transactional was misleading.
“Every nation ultimately acts out of national self-interest, rather than pure altruism or shared values,” he said.
The current friction, in his view, is part of a normal negotiation between two sovereign powers, not proof that the partnership was failing.
Besides Russian oil, another potential area of complication is the Trump administration suspending a scheme allowing US companies to sponsor skilled foreign workers.
On October 8, the Trump administration suspended new and pending applications under the US Permanent Labor Certification (Perm) program at several technology companies amid investigations into alleged visa fraud and the displacement of US workers.
The process is a key step for employers seeking permanent residency for foreign staff, including Indian professionals.
Harsh Pant, vice president for studies and foreign policy at the Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation (ORF), said Trump’s own words and actions had damaged ties despite regular high-level engagement.
“Even as he calls Prime Minister Modi a good friend, he has damaged the relationship by targeting India, and his supporters have been targeting Indians,” Pant told DW.
Pant said inconsistent messaging from Washington was eroding trust and could have consequences well beyond Trump’s presidency.
“The sense that America is unreliable, that America can’t be trusted, is beginning to come back into policy discourse,” he said.
The damage, he warned, could reach beyond government-to-government relations to Indian students, professionals and the middle class, whose goodwill has helped sustain ties through earlier disagreements.
“If public sentiment goes against a country, then it becomes very difficult for the policy-makers to craft an alternative policy,” Pant said, adding that US actions affecting Indian students and professionals “will have consequences.”

item.title: UN: More than 250,000 displaced within Yemen since fighting flared
item.description:
More than 250,000 people have been internally displaced in Yemen since the civil war reignited, the United Nations said Tuesday.
Yemen’s civil war -- in which a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Iran-backed Houthis -- reignited in July, months into the US-Iran conflict that has plunged the Middle East into crisis.
After an uneasy, four-year truce, Yemen’s conflict has surged back to life and then intensified when the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.
Displacement is continuing to rise sharply across Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, which was already suffering a vast humanitarian crisis.
“UNHCR is obviously deeply concerned about the escalating displacement situation,” Matthew Saltmarsh, spokesman for the UN refugee agency, told a press conference in Geneva.
“The numbers displaced have now reached over 250,000.
“These are people who have been internally displaced in Yemen between August 1 and October 17.”
Around half of those newly displaced are being hosted in Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.
Houthi fighters have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, interim capital of the Saudi-backed, internationally-recognized government.
“The most immediate needs that we’ve been able to identify are around shelter, food, and multi-purpose cash assistance, said Saltmarsh.
The spokesman noted that as of Saturday, some 3,836 new arrivals had been recorded in Djibouti, and a further 242 in Somalia, including both refugees and returnees.
Following the capsizing of a boat travelling from Djibouti to Yemen on the night of October 8-9, 139 bodies have been recovered, including 109 who have been identified, he said.
Meanwhile 82 survivors have been identified and were receiving support.

item.title: UN says 19m Afghans facing acute food insecurity by April
item.description:
The number of people facing acute food insecurity in Afghanistan is set to rise to 19.2 million during the winter season between November and April, the United Nations said Tuesday.
The food crisis in Afghanistan is projected to affect millions of children in 2027, the UN humanitarian agency Ocha said.
Between September and October, 15.9 million people -- or nearly one in three Afghans -- were facing food insecurity at crisis levels or worse, including 3.4 million in emergency conditions, the agency said.
But the outlook is set to deteriorate further.
“The number facing acute food insecurity is projected to rise to 19.2 million, of which five million are expected to face emergency levels of hunger,” which is “one step away from famine,” said Ocha’s Afghanistan spokeswoman Olga Cherevko.
The food crisis in Afghanistan is not simply about whether the food is available, but also about whether people can afford it, she told a press briefing in Geneva, speaking from Kabul.
The latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification snapshot projects that more than four million children aged six months to five years old will need treatment for acute malnutrition next year.
“Over one million of these children are expected to suffer severe acute malnutrition,” said Cherevko.
“These numbers represent children whose parents cannot afford nutritious food, and families whose ability to cope has been worn down by years of conflict, economic hardship, drought and other shocks.”
However, around one-third of nutrition sites across the country have closed or have suspended services, “largely due to funding cuts.”
“Once these services disappear, the consequences could be irreversible, particularly for children.”

item.title: Saudi says intercepted Houthi missile, blasts heard in capital
item.description:
Saudi forces on Tuesday said they had intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile aimed at the kingdom’s capital, after authorities issued a danger warning and AFP journalists reported hearing blasts.
The kingdom “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh,” said Turki Al-Malki, a spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition backing Yemen’s government in its war against the Houthis.
Riyadh was shaken by two blasts, according to AFP journalists in the capital.
“A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh City to alert for a potential danger,” the Saudi civil defense said in a statement on X.
But the alert was lifted a few minutes later, with the civil defense saying “the danger has passed.”
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have reached an unprecedented scale, forcing the postponement of a major investment conference in a blow to Riyadh’s hopes of attracting greater foreign capital and diversifying its economy.
The deadly attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis have forced Riyadh airport to shut.
The Saudi air force has been regularly targeting the group in retaliation amid fighting inside Yemen between the Houthis and the country’s Riyadh-backed government.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen’s capital Sanaa in defiance of Riyadh’s control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before uprooting Yemeni government forces from positions along the Red Sea coastline in a lightning campaign in September.
